# bats

## Goals

bats must be:

1. **The bats compiler**: Self-hosting bats compiler written in Bats. The old Rust implementation is archived at `/home/moshez/src/bats-lang/bats-old/`.

2. **Safe**: `unsafe = false` (or no `unsafe` key) in `bats.toml`. No `$UNSAFE begin...end` blocks in bats source. No `$extfcall` — it is an unsafe construct. C code belongs in library packages (file, process, sha256, etc.) that expose safe typed APIs. If a package must be `unsafe = true`, keep the unsafety minimal — expose safe wrappers so dependents can be `unsafe = false`. Being in an unsafe package is not carte blanche to add more unsafety.

## Build & Test

```bash
dist/debug/bats check --repository /home/moshez/src/bats-lang/repository-prototype
dist/debug/bats build --repository /home/moshez/src/bats-lang/repository-prototype
```

## Bootstrap seed

`bootstrap/c/` is the checked-in C output of the compiler (`bats build --to-c`), normalized by `scripts/bootstrap-c.sh` so it is byte-identical on every machine. It is the only thing needed to get a working `bats` from scratch:

```bash
cp -R bootstrap/c /tmp/seed && make -C /tmp/seed debug/bats
```

Every change to `src/` or `bats.lock` must commit a regenerated `bootstrap/c` in the same PR. A worker does not run the local regeneration (a long run, which is a CI job): it pushes the change, and when the step "Verify bootstrap/c matches sources" fails, the run uploads the tree it regenerated as the artifact `bootstrap-c-regenerated-<head sha>`. Download it, copy it over `bootstrap/c`, commit and push; the next run verifies it (`.claude/rules/runtime-header.md`, "Getting the regenerated tree from CI"):

```bash
gh run download <run id> --name bootstrap-c-regenerated-<head sha> --dir /tmp/bootstrap-c-new
rm -rf bootstrap/c && cp -R /tmp/bootstrap-c-new bootstrap/c
```

`scripts/bootstrap-c.sh dist/debug/bats ../repository-prototype` is the command the artifact is made by.

CI builds the compiler from `bootstrap/c`, regenerates, and fails if the result differs. It also checks the fixpoint (the compiler built by itself emits the same C). Never edit `bootstrap/c/` by hand.

## Architecture

Entry point: `src/bin/bats.bats`


## Workflow

All changes, even one byte, in ANY repo in bats-lang, must go through branch -> PR -> green -> merge. NEVER commit directly to main. Use `gh pr merge --merge` (no squash).

When creating a new repo: push an empty initial commit to main first (`git commit --allow-empty -m "Initial commit" && git push -u origin main`), then create a feature branch for the actual content. The first branch you push becomes the default, so main must exist before any feature branches.

Never blocked by another PR — add finishing that PR to the task list instead.

Never ask permission to keep going. Keep going until the success criterion is met.

Never wait. A PR in flight (CI running, a package publishing, a review pending) is never a reason to stop or idle: pick up the next independent task from the task list (this project always has one) and come back to the PR when its event arrives. Stopping is only for a decision that is the user's to make.

## Allowed Divergences from old Rust bats

These are the only allowed divergences. All other flags and behaviors must match the old Rust bats exactly.

Each divergence is kept with the notes of the area it is in, in `.claude/rules/` (the index at the end of this file names them; each loads when a file it covers is touched).

## Safety Enforcement

Unsafe constructs are detected by the lexer and **enforced** before patsopt runs, as are the rules that no `implement` is on a call cycle that no `implement` replaces what another package implements, and that an `implement` of another package's template is for a type of the implementing package. They, and `%{ ... %}` blocks, are rejected outside `$UNSAFE begin...end` blocks in ALL packages — both safe and unsafe. `$UNSAFE begin...end` blocks themselves are rejected in `unsafe = false` packages.

## Problem Resolution

A problem already existing is never a good reason to ignore it. Problems must be fixed. Safety problems must be prioritized.

## Safety Philosophy

Never add runtime checks (assertions, bounds checks at runtime, abort-on-overflow). The type system must prevent bad states at compile time. If you cannot prove safety statically, the API is wrong — fix the API, don't add a runtime check. Runtime checks are a sign that the type system is not being used correctly. The whole point of ATS2 and Bats is that safety is enforced by the compiler, not by runtime guards.

Segfaults must never happen. A segfault means something is fundamentally wrong — do not work around it, do not accept it, do not split files to avoid it. Find the root cause and fix it systemically. If it's caused by unbounded recursion, figure out how ATS2 is supposed to handle this (it has tail-call optimization). Use web search to understand the correct solution. Do not settle for less than correct.

Don't guess. Don't "try" things. Read the code. Carefully reason about what is happening. Understand before acting.

Do not assume Linux. Code must be portable (macOS, Linux, BSDs). Do not use `/proc/self/exe` or other Linux-specific paths.

Do not use bats-old unless it's an emergency. The self-hosting compiler is the primary build tool.

Fix problems regardless of size. Never say "too large for this session" or defer work. Do the work.

## We write bats, not shell

Our own code is bats. The only non-bats code is what is impossible in bats (the `make` of `bootstrap/c`), a dependency's own format, or a third-party tool used as it is. A workflow `run:` step that does more than call one bats subcommand or one third-party tool is code we wrote.

Review question: a PR that adds non-bats code of ours (a shell script, or a workflow `run:` step that is more than one call) is rejected unless it names the avenue it exhausted.

## Task Rules

A task should never be more than one thing: if it requires the word "and", for example, it should be broken up. If it refers to plurals, it should be broken up. If it has a comma, it should be broken up.

## CI is pinned

Every input to CI is pinned in the source (bats-lang/repository-prototype#269),
so a commit that passes keeps passing:

* `bats.lock` is committed, and CI unpacks exactly the locked versions.
* The seed compiler is `bootstrap/c`, in the tree.
* The package repository is fetched at the commit in
  `.github/repository-version`, so what the fixture tests under `tests/`
  lock (`bats lock` against it, e.g. `lock-namespace`) is pinned too.
* `relock-pins.yml` in bats-lang/repository-prototype is called by commit.

Pins move only through a reviewed pull request that runs the same CI.
The daily `relock.yml` (the shared `relock-pins.yml`) relocks against the
newest repository, moves `.github/repository-version` to it, pushes
`relock/<date>`, opens a pull request listing the old and new versions
and dispatches `check.yml` on it, so a breaking publish shows as a red
relock pull request and main stays green. GITHUB_TOKEN cannot change
workflow files, so without a `RELOCK_TOKEN` secret that pull request lists
a workflow pin that would move instead of moving it.

## Area notes

The notes are in `.claude/rules/`, each with `paths:` frontmatter, so a note loads only when a file it covers is touched. Each keeps its decisions, the research behind them, and what is proved apart from what is only tested.

A comment states its reason in one line and names the area by keyword; the detail lives in `.claude/rules/*.md`: search them for the keyword before changing the code.

request and main stays green. GITHUB_TOKEN cannot change workflow files,
so without a `RELOCK_TOKEN` secret that pull request lists a workflow pin
that would move instead of moving it: move it in a pull request of its

# pwa

pwa writes the shell around a Bats WASM app: the PWA's `index.html`,
`manifest.json`, `bridge.js` and service worker, and the Capacitor
project of its Android app.

## pwa emits no JS logic

JS lives only in bridge, as thin atoms (each with its `*_available`,
its answers decoded into datatypes), and the app's logic lives in the
app, in Bats, on those atoms (bats-lang/pwa#49).

* The page's one script is bridge's (`bridge.js`); `index.html` holds no
  inline script, and no element, class or attribute of pwa's own
  (`pwa-*`, `data-pwa-*`) that a script would act on.
* The service worker is bridge's (`produce_service_worker`), share
  target included: pwa adds no handler to it.
* The Android activity (`MainActivity.java`) runs no JS of its own: it
  calls bridge's entry points, `globalThis.batsNative.deliverFile(url,
  name)` for a file it hands over and `globalThis.batsNative.key(name)`
  for a volume key, one call each, and reads their answer. It calls one
  only once `batsNative` exists (a share can start the app before its
  page has loaded bridge.js); until then the answer is false.

## Changes to pwa

Further changes to pwa are disallowed: the only modifications allowed
are bug fixes (current functionality that misbehaves) or adding new
platforms (iOS, Electron, …). A feature the app needs from the platform
is a bridge atom and the app's own code, never pwa's.

## We write bats, not shell

Our own code is bats; the only non-bats code is what is impossible in bats, a dependency's own format, or a third-party tool used as it is.
A workflow `run:` step that does more than call one bats subcommand or one third-party tool is code we wrote.

## CI is pinned

Every input to CI is pinned in the source (bats-lang/repository-prototype#269),
so a commit that passes keeps passing:

* `bats.lock` is committed: CI never runs `bats lock` for the package, so
  `bats check` and `bats build` fetch exactly the locked versions, and fail
  when the lock is missing or does not match `bats.toml`. A library's lock
  pins only its own CI and tests; its dependents still resolve their own.
* The compiler is the commit in `.github/bats-version`, read by every
  workflow that builds bats (and by the publish workflow).
* The package repository is fetched at the commit in
  `.github/repository-version`, so what the test packages under `tests/`
  lock (`bats lock --dev`) is pinned too.
* `publish.yml` and `relock-pins.yml` in bats-lang/repository-prototype are
  called by commit, never `@main`.

Pins move only through a reviewed pull request that runs the same CI. The
daily `relock.yml` (the shared `relock-pins.yml`) relocks against the
newest, moves the compiler and repository pins, pushes `relock/<date>`,
opens a pull request listing the old and new versions and dispatches
`check.yml` on it, so a breaking publish shows as a red relock pull
request and main stays green. GITHUB_TOKEN cannot change workflow files,
so without a `RELOCK_TOKEN` secret that pull request lists a workflow pin
that would move instead of moving it: move it in a pull request of its
own. A pull request that needs newer packages runs `bats lock
--repository <dir>` and commits `bats.lock` (and
`.github/repository-version`) with the change.

The runner label is pinned too: every `runs-on` is `ubuntu-24.04`, never
`ubuntu-latest`, which moves when GitHub moves its default (bridge#154).
It is moved by hand, in a pull request of its own, when GitHub announces
the successor. quire's `android` job runs `android.yml` at the pwa commit
quire pins, so it picks up a new label only after quire moves that pin.

Which tool moves which pin (bats-lang/pwa#141, decided on
bats-lang/repository-prototype#367): Dependabot (`.github/dependabot.yml`,
weekly, a 7-day cooldown) moves the actions by commit with their release
comments, except the bats-lang ones, and the npm versions and lock of
`example/` (Playwright and serve). All of its updates arrive in one pull
request: `.github/dependabot.yml` has one `multi-ecosystem-groups` group,
`dependencies`, that the `npm` and `github-actions` entries join with
`multi-ecosystem-group: dependencies` and `patterns: ["*"]`, so a weekly run
opens one pull request for both ecosystems and one `check` run (owner ruling
on quire#795, quire#799; documentation:
https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/multi-ecosystem-updates).
The daily relock moves the compiler
(`.github/bats-version`), the package repository
(`.github/repository-version`) and the workflow pins of `publish.yml` and
`relock.yml`. Node's and Java's versions are in version files, never in a
workflow (keyword: version-file, bats-lang/pwa#136): `.nvmrc` (setup-node's
`node-version-file`) and `.java-version` (setup-java's `java-version-file`,
whose parser takes `21.0.12+8.0.LTS` from a file not named `.tool-versions`).
`android.yml` has no checkout of its caller, so it reads them from the
artifact it downloads, `app/<project-dir>/`, where `create_android_locked` writes them (the versions are two constants in
`src/lib.bats`); the caller's `upload-artifact` of the project needs
`include-hidden-files: true`, since the action skips dotfiles by default and
the job then fails with "node version file ... does not exist"; `e2e-setup` reads `.nvmrc` from its `working-directory`
(input `node-version-file`), `example/.nvmrc` for the example and the app's
own root file for quire, which moves to it with its next pin of this action.
A literal `node-version`, `java-version` or `python-version` in `.github` is
checked by bats `check-pins` (a `*-version-file` key is accepted, a literal
must be three numbers; bats#390). Until pwa#144's relock subcommand moves them, they are
moved by hand. quire takes its Node version from its own `.nvmrc`.
The bats
setup action's commit and the runner label are moved by hand, each in a
pull request of its own.

## Adversarial review before merge

No pull request merges before an adversarial review: a comment on the
pull request (its form is below), written by someone other than its
author (another agent or a person). The review first confirms the
pull request's kind from its diff, whatever the author called it.
A review knows three kinds: the two changes to pwa itself that "Changes
to pwa" allows (a bug fix, a new platform), and a change to process,
documentation or CI, which changes nothing pwa does:

* **A bug fix** (current functionality that misbehaves, against what it
  is documented to do): the review confirms it really is a deviation
  from the spec, that the fix is minimal, and that no capability slipped
  in: a "fix" that adds native behaviour, a plugin, a JS handler or
  anything else pwa did not do is reviewed as a capability, and so is
  refused unless it is a new platform.
* **A new platform** (iOS, Electron, …), the one new capability pwa
  takes: the review answers, with evidence (code, measurements, the
  platform's documentation):
  1. Is there no way to do this with what exists (bridge's atoms and the
     app's own Bats), at reasonable performance?
  2. Is this the minimal wrapper? Does each native piece map 1:1 to the
     platform's API? Why can it not be broken into smaller pieces, each
     a bridge atom? (Always asked; in detail when it is not 1:1.)
  3. Does the native side decide anything? It may only hand an event or
     a value to one of bridge's entry points (`batsNative`) and read its
     answer, as `MainActivity.java` does.

  The review analyzes the plausible alternatives and says why each
  would not work: a bridge atom on the web API the platform's web view
  already has, an existing entry point, the app doing it in Bats.

  Any other capability (a Capacitor plugin, native connectivity, native
  code pwa generates for a feature) gets `Verdict: changes needed`: a
  feature the app needs from the platform is a bridge atom and the
  app's own code, never pwa's.
* **Process, documentation or CI** changes: the review confirms they add
  no capability. Test tooling (gen-pwa test, which runs an app's suite)
  is process: the review confirms it changes nothing pwa generates and
  nothing the app runs.

Whatever its kind, a pull request that adds non-bats code of ours (a shell
script, any other non-bats file, or a workflow `run:` step that does more than
call one bats subcommand or one third-party tool) gets `Verdict: changes needed`
unless it names the avenue in bats it exhausted.

A DOM write is never pwa's: it is an opcode of bridge's diff stream,
issued by the app. App policy (which attributes, roles, defaults, when)
never lives in pwa's generated native code or page: it is the app's, in
Bats (bats-lang/pwa#49). A pull request that puts either in pwa gets
`Verdict: changes needed`.

When the only change since the approving review is a merge of main (keyword: main-merge, bats-lang/bats#426), the review of the new head is not a new adversarial review: run `bats merge-proof <reviewed-sha> <head>` at the root of a checkout of the head and paste the command's output as the head-naming review, inside a comment of the form below (its `Reviewed:` line names the new head in full, its one `Verdict:` line is `Verdict: approved` only when the output is the line `OK: ...`, and the output is plain text, on one line of its own); any other output (`NOT OK: ...`, or hunks alone) is read by the reviewer, who reviews the head as any other change.

### Who reviews, and where

Only a comment by a trusted author counts: its `author_association` is
OWNER, MEMBER or COLLABORATOR. These repositories are public, so anyone
else's comment, approving or not, is ignored; the gate's log names each
review attempt's author and association, and the status says "No review
by a trusted author" with the associations it saw. The reviewer is
another agent or person than the one that wrote the change: all agents
here post from one account, so the review is done by a separate
reviewer agent, named on its `Reviewer:` line.

A review that approves is a comment in the pull request's conversation,
not a formal pull request review and not a line comment. A formal review
by a trusted author can only block:

* its text is read like a comment's (as rendered), ordered with the
  comments by when it was submitted, so a formal review that is the
  newest review attempt makes the gate pending, whatever it says (the
  agents post from the pull request author's account, so their formal
  reviews can only be "Comment" reviews);
* one that requests changes (GitHub's "Request changes") stands, as
  GitHub's own rule does, until it is dismissed, whatever comments
  follow.

### The review comment

The gate reads each comment (and each formal review's text) twice: as written, and as GitHub renders it
(`body_text`, GitHub's own plain text of the comment), so what it judges
is what a reader sees. A comment is a review attempt when one of the
first three non-blank lines of either says "adversarial review", read
loosely: NFKC, no zero-width characters, BOM, combining marks or CR,
lower case, entities, escapes, link targets and marks dropped, digits
read as the letters they look like, any non-ASCII letter standing for
any letter, and up to two letters wrong. The newest attempt decides,
alone; an older one never counts again. It approves only when it is
perfectly formed:

* written, its first line is exactly `## Adversarial review`, and shown,
  its first line is `Adversarial review`;
* written and shown, it has exactly one line with `Verdict:` in it (or
  starting with the word), and that line is exactly `Verdict: approved`
  (or `Verdict: changes needed`): no bold, no indent, no trailing space
  or period, no other words;
* written, it has exactly one line with `Reviewed:` in it (or starting
  with the word), and that line is exactly `Reviewed: <SHA>`, the full
  40-character lowercase SHA of the pull request's head commit it
  reviewed; shown, that line is the same, with the SHA as GitHub
  shortens it (7 digits) or in full;
* written, its letters are ASCII, and it has no invisible (format)
  characters, no combining marks, no code fence (three backticks or
  three tildes, anywhere), no HTML comment, no HTML tag (`<` followed by
  a letter or `/`) and no link or footnote definition (a line starting
  `[…]:`). Reviews use inline code and plain text only.

A verdict is never edited: an edited review counts as no approval, and a
new verdict is a new comment. Anything short of the form above is
pending, whatever it says; the status's description says what is wrong.
Other comments should not say "adversarial review" in their first three
lines: such a comment is an attempt, and as the newest it makes the gate
pending.

### The gate

`.github/workflows/review-gate.yml` sets the commit status
`adversarial-review` on the pull request's head commit (read from the
pull request, exactly 40 lowercase hex digits, three tries): success
only for a perfectly formed, unedited approval of the current head in
the newest attempt by a trusted author, with no standing request for
changes. Anything else is pending, and so is any failure (an API error,
a parse error, any unexpected exit), so an earlier success never
outlives a failed run. A push after an approval turns it back to
pending, until a new review names the new head.

It runs on every pull request event (`pull_request_target`), every
comment created, edited or deleted (`issue_comment`), every formal
review submitted, edited or dismissed (through
`.github/workflows/review-gate-relay.yml`, which has no permissions and
does nothing: `pull_request_review` would run the pull request's own
copy of a workflow, so the relay's completion runs the gate through
`workflow_run`), and over every open pull request about every 15
minutes, best effort (`schedule`). All of them run the gate as the
default branch has it, never as the pull request has it; it checks out nothing and runs no code
of the pull request, which is what makes that safe. The relay is only a
fast path; correctness rests on the schedule. It uses no action, only
the runner's `gh` and `python3`.

Known limits:

* Any workflow or token with `statuses: write` can post an
  `adversarial-review` status, so a pull request that adds or changes a
  file in `.github/workflows` could forge one. Such a pull request is a
  process change, and its review must check exactly this: that no
  workflow it adds or changes can post the status or widen its
  permissions to do so, and that the gate and its relay stay as they
  are.
* A commit status belongs to a commit, not to a pull request: two pull
  requests with the same head commit share one `adversarial-review`
  status, set by whichever ran last.
* A pull request can change or delete its own copy of the relay, and a
  fork's runs can wait for "Approve and run": a formal review's effect
  then waits for the next comment, push or scheduled run.
* The schedule is about every 15 minutes, best effort: GitHub delays
  scheduled runs under load and sometimes drops them, and turns a public
  repository's schedules off after 60 days without activity; they stay
  off until someone enables the workflow again (Actions → review-gate →
  Enable workflow). A scheduled run and an event's run are not in one
  concurrency group, so a scheduled run that read the comments just
  before a new review can post after that review's own run, until the
  next run.
* A review attempt is seen only by its first three non-blank lines, and
  only its one Verdict line is judged: a header further down, or prose
  that contradicts the exact approved line, is not caught. Each needs a
  careless or bad-faith review that still writes the exact approved
  line.
* If every lookup of the head fails on a comment event, nothing can be
  marked; the next scheduled run decides.
* The gate checks the comment's form and its author's association, not
  which agent or person wrote it: under one account, the authoring
  agent could post a perfectly formed approval itself; and a header misspelt by more than two
  letters is not seen as an attempt.
* Deleting the newest review makes the one before it the newest again.
  So does editing a formal review: the API gives a formal review no edit
  time, so an edit is not detected, and a trusted reviewer who edits a
  blocking formal review so that it is no longer a review attempt makes
  the older approval the newest again.
* Dismissing a "Request changes" review ends the standing request, but
  not the review attempt its text is: while it is the newest attempt,
  the gate stays pending, and a new review comment is still needed.
* Line comments on the diff are not read: a review posted only as a
  line comment does not block.
* An organization member whose membership is private may show as
  CONTRIBUTOR to the workflow's token, so their reviews do not count:
  the gate's log shows the association it saw. Make the membership
  public, or add them as a collaborator.

`adversarial-review` must be made a required status check of `main` by
a repository admin (Settings → Branches → the rule for `main` →
Require status checks to pass before merging → add
`adversarial-review`); until then the gate only reports. The pull
request template (`.github/pull_request_template.md`) asks the author
the same questions; the reviewer checks the answers, not just their
presence.

## Feature notes

Each feature's notes are in a rules file under `.claude/rules/`, which loads when a file it
names is touched (its `paths:`):

* gen-pwa test (pwa#82): `.claude/rules/gen-pwa-test.md`
* gen-pwa pages (pwa#243): `.claude/rules/static-pages.md`
* gen-pwa values (pwa#244): `.claude/rules/public-values.md`
* The Android smoke test: `.claude/rules/android-smoke.md`
* The relock of the Android SDK pins (pwa#185): `.claude/rules/android-relock.md`
* The e2e setup action (quire#637): `.claude/rules/e2e-setup.md`
* The Play release workflow (pwa#90, quire#623): `.claude/rules/play-release.md`
* Skipping a push run's tests when the merge queue passed the same commit (pwa#215): `.claude/rules/queue-passed.md`
* The signing key's fingerprints (pwa#96, quire#623): `.claude/rules/key-fingerprints.md`
* The Android build's retry on a dependency resolution failure, `android-sdk-pins build-again` (pwa#276): `.claude/rules/android-gradle-retry.md`

A comment states its reason in one line and names the area by keyword; the detail lives in `.claude/rules/*.md`: search them for the keyword before changing the code.

---
name: worker
description: Worker on one bats-lang/quire ticket. Use for any ticket to fix or build in quire. Carries what is quire's; the brief names the ticket, files and check.
---

You are a worker on bats-lang/quire. The brief names the ticket, the files and docs to read, the kind of change and the check to run. The rules of a worker that hold for any project (the ticket is the standard, one ticket in one PR, design check, evidence, hand-back, checkouts, short local runs) are in pitboss's sweep skill, `plugins/pitboss/skills/sweep/references/rules.md` ("Briefs and workers", "Tickets", "Reviews", "Checkouts and disk") and `engineering.md` of dev-skill-up/pitboss, a manual copy at pitboss commit 71ffe84, paths changed (quire's `CLAUDE.md`, "Pitboss's sweep skill"). Read them first. What follows is what names quire's, bats's or pwa's files, tools and CI.

## Design

- Data read into one value (a string, a buffer, an array) has a size that value can hold; say the bound or stream it. The one exception is a stored format (the shelf and layout of `library.bats`, where the number is the stored value).

## Tests

- A test failure that gets a p0 ticket is quarantined in the commit that files it: `test.fixme('#N ...')` on every project (`.claude/rules/e2e.md`, "Quarantine and race fixes"). The fix removes the mark, and the PR body lists it in a line `Quarantine: ...`.
- A fix for a race (a failure that depends on the runner's speed, a fixed wait or an order of events) merges only when its PR body has a line `Race: ...` and the three items of that section, each a line of its own: `Root cause: ...`, `Injection: ...` (the raw output is in Evidence) and `CI run: <URL>`. No test is repeated to count failures. No new `waitForTimeout` or sleep in `e2e/`: wait for an event.

## Where you work, and how long a run is

- **Short jobs run locally, CI runs the rest** (the owner's words, as quoted in quire#911, filed 2026-10-26T17:49:33Z: "I said "no long jobs", not "try to find clever ways to run them". Short jobs locally, CI for the rest"): a check that takes more than a few minutes locally is left to CI, not run here (foreground or background, whole or split); you commit, push when the push rule below allows, and CI is the evidence, named in the PR body as CI's; nothing is left running at hand-back. What runs locally is incremental, in that checkout, and finishes in a few minutes: a named fixture or one shard of a population (fixtures, specs, tests); the rest of the population is CI's, and the PR body says so. No two heavy runs at once on this 4-core machine.
- The check command is the one in `.claude/rules/ci.md`, "Checking locally before a push": `BATS_SLOTS=1` through the env file, no `timeout` wrapper. The first build of a new checkout is cold and takes longer than a few minutes, so it is left to CI: the next ticket is a new branch in a warm checkout, and a push from a cold one is checked by CI.
- In quire, a worktree you make with `git worktree add` has the pre-push checks installed: the sweep (`qsweep`) sets `core.hooksPath .githooks` in the repository's own config, which every worktree inherits (`.claude/rules/ci.md`, "The pre-push hook"; the sweep prints `HOOKS-NOT-INSTALLED` for a checkout whose effective value differs, and a `--no-verify` is never used). Push with `qsweep push`, which reads `~/quire.env` for the hook's variables; write `bats.pin` once beside each compiler you have (`.claude/rules/ci.md`).
- **Affected (quire#957 and #1006, keyword: affected).** Before every push, run `python3 scripts/ci-groups.py local $(git merge-base origin/main HEAD) --run <repository>` for your diff (quire). It lists the whole selected population on standard output (`check`, `checkers`, the fixtures `bats fixtures tests/static --list-affected` lists for the paths of your diff, every e2e spec the rule selects), which is CI's affected rule with bats's own fixture selection, not a list you build with `grep`. It needs the package repository (`--run <repository>` or `BATS_REPOSITORY`) and `QUIRE_STATIC_WORK` set in the env file, so that bats's memo is kept; without a memo bats lists every fixture, and a bats that fails fails the command. You run from the list only what finishes in a few minutes (the rule above): `check`, `checkers` and a named fixture or spec; the rest of the list is CI's, and CI's run is the evidence for it. The PR's Evidence has the command and its output.
- A local e2e run needs tracefs, and a restarted container may have none (quire#958): when the preflight says `no tracefs instances directory`, run once `grep -q tracefs /proc/mounts || mount -t tracefs nodev /sys/kernel/tracing` (the allowed command; `.claude/rules/ci.md`, quire#765) and run the spec again. Run no other `mount`.
- Reject expects are written with `bats fixtures --bless` (bats#522) after the last edit of a module, never by hand and never by repeated population runs. Until bats#522 merges, write each from the observed error of one run of that snippet.

## Pushing and the PR body

- Push with `qsweep push <git push arguments>`: it prints `qsweep pressure` and runs `git push` only when it says `runner pressure: none` (exit 0). If `qsweep pressure` exits non-zero, hand back at once, naming where you stopped and the SHA of what is unpushed; never loop, retry or sleep for the pressure to clear (owner, 2026-10-25T17:58:35Z, transcript line 95384, on a loop of `qsweep pressure` and `sleep 60`: "Runner pressure should cause hand back, not whatever this is"). A pressure hold never empties an agent row: the orchestrator pushes your commit when the hold ends and starts the next item.
- The PR body's first line is `Fixes #N`, it has a line `Head: <the 40-character SHA>` that is the head, an `Evidence` section, and it ends with the line `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code)`; the session's GitHub proxy replaces that line with the footer `_Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code)_` when the body is written through `gh api`, and the lint accepts either. `python3 tests/static/guidelines.py --pr-body <file> --head <sha>` checks the form, and `.github/workflows/text-lint.yml` (the shared lint of repository-prototype, called by commit) runs the form of the body on every push and edit. After every push, edit the body for the new head.

# quire

## Pitboss's sweep skill

The rules of the process that hold for any project (research before design, a proof is a proof, comments name their area by keyword, names are words, the priorities and the order of work, no shell of our own and no mtimes in freshness, breaking changes with one version of overlap, CI pinned, no cache key relied on, check before a push, evidence, red tests and CI, the version is the commit's, and the standing rules of the orchestrator, the worker and the reviewer) are in pitboss's sweep skill, `plugins/pitboss/skills/sweep/` of dev-skill-up/pitboss: `references/rules.md`, `references/engineering.md`, `references/ci.md` and `references/adversarial-review.md`. Quire's copy is a manual copy at pitboss commit 71ffe84, paths changed; this file and `.claude/` hold only what is quire's, bats's or pwa's. When the copy moves, this commit is changed in the same pull request.

## Decisions are made by research, not left to the human

The quality rules below (the proofs, the static tests, the e2e suite) still hold: when a choice would break one, choose another that keeps it.

## A proof is a proof

Trusted primitives live in the one package that owns the platform, state what they assume, and are tested there; nothing in quire uses `praxi`, `assume` or `$UNSAFE` to skip a proof. Where the proof system cannot reach (the array package had no model of an array's contents), the tool is extended (a content-indexed array API in the array package), not worked around at runtime.

## Names are words

Element ids and numbered-id prefixes (up to 16 bytes) are named in words too: `search-close`, `toc-row12`, not `qsrz`. Terse names collide (a rename of the id `qn` once also hit a query length of the same name).

## Priorities

The priorities (p0 to p3) and the order of work are in the reference, `rules.md`, "Tickets" and "Agents and slots". Quire's own rule on top of them:

The Android release is not a priority. Priority is the order in which tickets
are worked, and p2 means user-visible features and developer experience, not
"held for the release". If the owner holds the Android release for an issue,
that hold is a rule on top of the order: it is recorded on the issue, and it
does not move the issue to another priority.

## Pipeline and tooling improvements belong in bats or pwa

Anything a second app would copy is built where the apps share it, and quire calls it:
the compiler's build, cache and fixture runner, and the setup of the toolchain, are bats's
(bats-lang/bats); the Android project and its release, test running (Playwright, its
install and browsers), the emulator job and the pages beside the app are pwa's
(bats-lang/pwa). Quire's own CI holds what is about quire: its specs and fixtures, which
job runs which (`tests/groups.json`), its books and its proofs. Before a workflow or
script of quire is changed, ask whether an alarm clock built the same way would copy the
change; if it would, the change is a ticket in bats or pwa first (quire#623 is the list of
what already is one), and quire's change is only the call.

A stopgap in quire is allowed only when waiting would cost more than the move (a flake that
removes a merge queue entry each time it happens), and then the ticket that moves it is
written first, the stopgap says so in its comment, and it is deleted when the move lands
(quire#635's retries and cache, moved by quire#637). A stopgap with no ticket for its move
is not a fix. The rule against shell and other non-bats code of our own (quire#646, quire#731) is in the reference, `engineering.md` and `ci.md`.

## Breaking changes keep at least one published version of overlap (#762)

The rule is in the reference (`rules.md`, "Published APIs") and in repository-prototype's CLAUDE.md, under "Publishing Packages" (https://github.com/bats-lang/repository-prototype/blob/20f15c0/CLAUDE.md, bats-lang/repository-prototype#381 and #384). The brief templates carry the line (`.claude/orchestration.md`, "Briefs and the machine"), and `tests/static/guidelines.py` refuses a brief or a review of a signature change that lacks it.

## CI is pinned

Every input to CI is pinned in the source (#203), so a commit that passes keeps passing:
the packages by the committed `bats.lock`, the compiler by its commit in
`.github/bats-version`, pwa's Android workflow by its commit (`android.yml@<sha>` in
`check.yml`), and the runner image by its label. A quire PR that adopts new package
versions runs `bats lock --repository <dir>` and commits `bats.lock` with the change that
needs them. The build cache and its key, the merge queue, the Node packages, the mutation
check and which groups a change runs are in `.claude/rules/ci.md`, which loads when CI files
are touched.

Quire still has `.github/dependabot.yml`, which #996 removes once quire's `relock.yml` uses the relock's moves of actions, npm packages and the Gradle wrapper (repository-prototype#392, #414 to #416). Until then, which tool moves which pin (`.github/dependabot.yml`, weekly, a 7-day cooldown, one pull request
for all the updates of both ecosystems, from one `multi-ecosystem-groups` group with `patterns:
["*"]`: "Define groups that span multiple package ecosystems to get a single Dependabot pull
request", https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/multi-ecosystem-updates;
#760, #795, the detail in `.claude/rules/ci.md`, "Node's packages"): the daily relock moves
the compiler, the package repository and the workflow pins it names. Dependabot moves quire's
actions by commit with their release comments, except the `bats-lang/*` ones, and the npm versions
and `package-lock.json` of the root `package.json`, which carries `@playwright/test` and so the
Chromium it runs. The bats setup action's commit and the runner label are moved by hand, each in a
pull request of its own.

## No cache key is relied on for correctness (#622)

Bats drops a `build/` whose stamp (its own inputs, ATS2, the C compiler, the flags, the target)
differs and says so on stderr, rebuilds a module by the content hash of its sources and of the
files patsopt read, and serves a fixture's memo only when every file it read is unchanged
(bats's CLAUDE.md and its `stamp`, `build-freshness`, `check-memo` and `fixtures-memo` notes).
Quire's key is `quire-<name>@<commit>`, only a locator for the newest earlier cache; it names
no pin, image, lock or source hash and carries no number to bump, so a new input needs no key
edit. What bats does not yet judge is listed in `.claude/rules/ci.md`.

## Check locally before every push

Run `bats check` before every push when it is incremental (seconds to minutes), so a push that
does not type-check never reaches CI. Short jobs run locally and CI runs the rest (quire#911, the
owner's words in `.claude/agents/worker.md`): the first build of a new checkout is cold (10 to 15
minutes) and is left to CI, not started here (foreground or background), and so is any other check
that takes more than a few minutes; nothing is left running at hand-back. Under disk pressure `qsweep clean` removes only
an older worktree whose pull request merged, never the one that merged last, a ticket in
flight, or the orchestrator's checkout. How (the compiler, the machine's slots and env file,
the cache, the e2e run): `.claude/rules/ci.md`.

## Evidence, red tests and CI

The rules for the agents are in `.claude/agents/worker.md`, `.claude/agents/reviewer.md` and
`.claude/orchestration.md`, and `tests/static/guidelines.py` (the `checkers` group) refuses
the phrases that made these mistakes come back (quire#751).

## The version is the commit's

How quire's version is made and shown: `.claude/rules/release.md`.

## Play release

A push to main that passes the whole check is released to Google Play's internal testing
track by `check.yml`'s `play-internal` job; production is a promotion in the Play Console
(details: `.claude/rules/release.md`).
